1324.title: Praying for the dead
1324.hook: many Christians pray for the dead; others entrust them to God
1324.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries of a death and in the Mass or Divine Liturgy; in Protestant churches that do not, the dead are commended to God and the service gives thanks for their life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, funerals: two rooms, two moods, one hope underneath. Your line was memory eternal.

Carved at the bottom of an old headstone, under the name and dates, worn soft by rain: R.I.P. It can read like a goodbye. Sleep tight. It's over now. But ask who those letters are talking to. Not the dead person, exactly, and not quite the people walking past. Rest in peace is a request. Somebody is being asked to give that rest. The question under the stone: once someone has died, is there anything left to say to God about them?

First, the words. R.I.P. stands for the Latin requiescat in pace, may he or she rest in peace: a prayer, shortened to fit on stone. Second, those who pray. Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries, at Mass or the Divine Liturgy. An old Catholic prayer asks God to give them eternal rest and let perpetual light shine on them. Orthodox services ask God to give rest to the soul of his servant, where there is no pain or sorrow. They point to Second Maccabees, a book in their Bibles, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died, and the book praises praying for the dead. And Paul writes of his friend Onesiphorus: "The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." Some readers think Onesiphorus had already died; the letter doesn't say. Third, those who entrust. Protestants who follow the Reformers don't pray for the dead. They hold that a person who has died is already safe in God's hands, and nothing needs adding. They can lean on Revelation: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." Rest, already given. So at the grave they give thanks, and let go. Fourth, look at both: one keeps speaking to God about the person, one places the person in God's hands. Both refuse to treat death as the end of God's care. Rest in peace can be either: a prayer, or a hand opening.

Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you still carry, the way they stood or laughed. If you pray for the dead, ask God to give them rest; if you entrust instead, place them in God's hands; if you don't pray, hold them in your thoughts, then open your hands a little. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Praying for the dead. Some Christians keep praying for those who have died; others entrust them to God and give thanks.
Your line: rest in peace. Three letters, and a request inside them. That's today, done.

1325.title: The resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:35–44)
1325.hook: sown a seed, raised a plant: perishable to imperishable
1325.tomorrow: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)
1325.howItsDone: Christians confess the resurrection of the body in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, and 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings offered for funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for the dead: some Christians keep praying, others entrust the dead to God. Your line was rest in peace.

"How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?" That's not a skeptic's heckle from today. Paul puts it in the mouth of "some man" in a letter to the church in Corinth. It's a fair question. If a body is buried and returns to dust, what comes back? The same knees? The same scar? A body at eighty, or at twenty? People in Corinth seem to have found it hard to picture. Paul's reply starts bluntly, "Thou fool," but he doesn't leave it there. He answers with something you could hold in your palm: a seed.

First, the seed. Paul says "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die," and "thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain." You don't plant a wheat stalk. You plant a small dry kernel, and what comes up looks nothing like it. Yet it's the same life: what goes into the ground and what rises belong to each other. Second, God is good at bodies. People, animals, birds and fish all have different flesh. The sun, the moon and the stars each have their own glory, and "one star differeth from another star in glory." The God who made that much variety, Paul is saying, can make a new kind of body too. Third, the list: "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power." Each line is a before and an after. Fourth, the surprising phrase: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." Not a ghost, and not a body made of fog. Some readers take it to mean a body fully alive with God's Spirit, still a body, but no longer headed for the grave. The creed in the Book of Common Prayer doesn't say the soul floats on; it says "the Resurrection of the body." Christians hold a hope with the same shape as the seed: real continuity, real change.

If you have a seed handy, an apple pip or a bean, hold it in your palm; if not, picture one, small and dry, looking nothing like what it will become. Set one person you've lost beside it in your mind. If you pray, read Paul's line slowly, sown in weakness, raised in power; if not, simply hold the seed and wonder.
The resurrection body. Paul's picture of the body raised by God: sown like a seed, perishable, and raised imperishable, a spiritual body.
Your line: sown, raised. The same life, coming up as a changed body. Until tomorrow.

1326.title: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)
1326.howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 15 is read in the burial service of the Book of Common Prayer, and its taunt to death is sung in Handel's Messiah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resurrection body: a seed goes into the ground, and something new comes up. Your line was sown, raised.

For most of a long chapter, Paul has been arguing in careful steps: if this, then that, seeds and stars and the order of things. Then, near the end, the argument breaks open. He turns, the way someone turns on a bully who has finally lost his grip, and speaks straight to death. Not about death. To it. He calls it by name, the way you'd call across a schoolyard, and asks it a mocking question. It's short, and it's fierce.

Here are the lines: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" First, they're borrowed. Paul echoes the prophet Hosea, where the King James has God say: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction." Readers of Hosea argue over whether that line is a promise or a threat in its own chapter. In Paul's hands, it's a taunt. Second, the sting. Paul's Greek word can mean an insect's stinger, or the sharp goad a farmer used to drive an ox: the point that does the damage. And Paul names that point: "The sting of death is sin." Some readers hear in that line that the hurt of death isn't only the ending; it's everything left broken, unforgiven, undone. Third, thanks: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying. He claims death has already lost, because of the resurrection the whole chapter is about. Its point has been pulled. Fourth, the taunt ends in work. The very next verse: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." Not a shout and then a nap; a shout, and then back to the job. Long after, the poet John Donne caught the same nerve in a sonnet that tells Death not to be proud, and ends by saying that death itself shall die.
screen: `THE STING IS THE POINT THAT HURTS.`

segments.voice: Let one fear come up, about death or something smaller that feels like a little death, losing a job, a friend, getting older, and look at it squarely. If you pray, say Paul's line to it quietly, where is thy sting; if you don't, ask the fear a question back instead of only listening to it. Notice whether it shrinks, even a little.

1327.title: Heaven comes down
1327.hook: not escape to the clouds, but heaven and earth renewed
1327.howItsDone: Christians pray "thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven" in the Lord's Prayer, and some churches link the hope of a new creation with caring for the earth, through creation-care ministries or a season of prayer for creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, O death: Paul's taunt, borrowed from Hosea, and then back to work. Your line was where is your sting?

A cartoon in a magazine: a man in a white robe sits alone on a cloud, holding a harp, looking bored. The joke works because the picture is familiar. Heaven, in it, is somewhere up and away, thin and misty, where souls float off once the body is done, and the earth is left behind like an old coat. Now open the last pages of the Bible and watch which way things move. John doesn't see anyone floating up. He sees something coming down.
screen: `A MAN ON A CLOUD WITH A HARP.`

segments.voice: First, the direction. John writes: "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven." Down. God's home arrives on earth, and a voice says "the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them." The ending isn't people leaving the world. It's God moving in. Second, the prayer Christians already pray. In the Lord's Prayer, Jesus teaches, "Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." Not take us out of the earth; bring heaven's way into it. Third, creation waiting. Paul writes to Rome that "the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now," and hopes that "the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption." Not only people: the whole created world, waiting to be set free. Isaiah had said it long before: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth." Fourth, the word. A couple of weeks ago this block heard Paul say that anyone in Christ "is a new creature." The Greek behind that, kainē ktisis, can just as well be translated new creation. The same hope runs from one person to the whole world: not thrown away, made new. Christians hold these pictures in different balances. Some speak mostly of heaven as where the faithful go at death. Others stress that God will renew this earth itself. Some hold both: rest with God now, and a renewed creation at the end. What the Bible's last pages add is the direction. Heaven comes down.
screen: `IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Notice what's right around you: the floor under your feet, the air, a plant, the view through a window. In this hope, all of it is worth making new, not throwing away. If you pray, you can say the line from the Lord's Prayer, thy will be done in earth; if not, just let your attention rest on the ground under you.
New creation. The hope that God doesn't throw the world away but makes it new, heaven and earth renewed, God dwelling with people.
Your line: heaven comes down. This earth isn't an old coat to leave behind. See you tomorrow.

1328.title: Seeing God
1328.hook: Catholic and Orthodox writers speak of seeing God face to face as our joy
1328.tomorrow: Not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13)
1328.howItsDone: Catholic teaching names the vision of God as the final happiness of the saints; Orthodox prayer and icons speak of beholding the uncreated light; Protestant hymns and sermons speak of seeing Christ face to face.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new creation: the holy city coming down, not souls floating up. Your line was heaven comes down.

Hold up a spoon and look into the bowl of it. There you are, upside down, blurred, the color off. It's you, but not clearly. Paul reaches for a picture like that when he writes to Corinth about what comes at the end: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Behind that line stands an old refusal. Moses, who had seen the burning bush and the sea split open, once asked God, "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." And God answered, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live."

First, the refusal. God sets Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with a hand while the glory passes by, and lets him see from behind. Not the face. Moses has to be hidden to be kept safe. Second, the promise. Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." The letter of John says, "we shall see him as he is." And Paul's glass, in the King James, is a mirror. Some readers say God is glimpsed now only in reflections, in scripture, in other people, in a sunset, never straight on. Then, face to face. Third, the name. Catholic theology calls this the beatific vision, from the Latin for the seeing that makes blessed. Seeing God isn't a reward handed out alongside other rewards; it is the joy itself. Thomas Aquinas, among others, taught that human longing finally comes to rest there. Orthodox writers speak of beholding the light of God, the light the disciples saw on the mountain when Jesus was transfigured, and of sharing in God's life. Protestant hymns sing of seeing Christ face to face. The churches haven't only used different words here; they have argued. Orthodox theology holds that God's essence stays beyond any creature, and the saints see and share God's uncreated light; Catholic theology speaks of seeing God's essence. Both place the joy in seeing God. Fourth, the seeing goes both ways. Paul finishes his sentence: "then shall I know even as also I am known." In Paul's line, being known comes first.

Close your eyes. If you pray, bring to mind the hope of seeing God's face, without picturing any features, only the sense of being looked at with love, and of looking back; if you don't, bring to mind the face of someone who has loved you well, and let yourself be seen by it. Either way, don't perform: just be seen.
Beatific vision. From the Latin, the seeing that makes blessed: the hope of seeing God face to face, as the joy itself.
Your line: face to face. No more blurred spoon. Same time tomorrow.

1329.title: Not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13)
1329.howItsDone: 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 is among the readings offered in some churches' funeral services, and some Christians speak of the dead as having fallen asleep in Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beatific vision: through a glass darkly now, then face to face. Your line was face to face.

Two words in the King James Bible: "Jesus wept." He has just asked where they laid his friend Lazarus, and they've answered, come and see. In John's telling he is about to call Lazarus out of the grave. He weeps anyway. Today's line is from Paul, writing to a young church in Thessalonica that had buried some of its own. This block met his sentence once already, read for what it says about the end. Today, read it for grief. It's easy to hear it as an order to stop crying. Read slowly, it says something else.

Here's the sentence: "But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." First, read it slowly. Paul doesn't say: don't sorrow. He says: don't sorrow even as, the same way as, those with no hope. Grief is assumed. He never asks them to stop crying; he asks what their tears are leaning on. His attention is on the church he's writing to, not on anyone else's grief. Second, the word asleep. Paul calls the dead them which are asleep. It's gentle, and it carries a hope inside it, because sleep is something you wake from. He goes on: "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." Third, back to Lazarus. In John's story, Jesus weeps knowing what he is about to do. The hope doesn't cancel the tears. It stands next to them. That's the shape Paul is asking for: tears, with something underneath. Fourth, grief kept company. Paul tells the church in Rome, "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Not explain to them. Not hurry them along. Weep with them. Christian grief, in these letters, is not quieter or tidier than anyone's. It cries, and it doesn't cry alone.

Bring to mind a loss, a person or something else you've had to let go of, and let yourself feel its weight without hurrying past it. If you pray, hold it alongside Paul's words, them which are asleep; if not, hold it alongside one good thing that loss left in you, a habit, a laugh, a way of seeing. Let the grief and the hope sit side by side, neither one winning. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Not as those without hope. Paul's phrase in First Thessalonians four: Christians grieve, and their grief leans on the hope of the resurrection.

1330.title: Watchful, not anxious
1330.hook: live each day ready and unafraid
1330.howItsDone: Churches that keep Advent watch toward Christ's coming in that season, and in vigils and night prayers; Gospel stories of watchful servants are among its readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not as those without hope: Paul assumes grief and asks what it leans on. Your line was grieve, with hope.

It's late. The house is quiet, but nobody's gone to bed. Lamps still lit, belts still fastened, shoes still on. The master of the house is at a wedding feast, and nobody knows when he'll be back. Midnight. Later. Toward morning. The servants aren't pacing or panicking. They're just awake, with the door within reach, so that the moment he knocks, it opens. Jesus tells this little scene in Luke's Gospel, and then adds a twist so strange it's easy to read right past it.

First, the instruction: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning." Dressed for action, lamp lit. In Mark, Jesus puts it in one word, and widens it: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." The Greek word behind watch means stay awake. Second, the twist. When the master gets home and finds them awake, "he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them." The master serves the servants. The one they've waited for waits on them. So watching isn't guarding against a punishment; it's staying up for someone who is coming home to feed you. Third, not anxious. The same Jesus says, "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." And Paul writes, "Be careful for nothing." In the King James, careful means full of care, anxious, not cautious. Anxiety stares at tomorrow. Watchfulness pays attention to now. Fourth, watching up close. In Gethsemane, Jesus takes three disciples a little way with him, asks them to watch with him, and goes on to pray. He comes back and finds them asleep: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" Then: "the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Watching there isn't scanning the horizon. It's staying with someone, awake, in the hour that's here. Readiness, in these stories, is attention to now, and the good in front of you, done well.

Notice if your mind is running ahead, to tomorrow, next month, the end of everything, and let it come back to this day. Ask what ordinary good is in front of you: a meal to cook, a kid to pick up, a call to return. If you pray, offer it to God as the thing you'd like to be found doing; if you don't, simply hold it with care.
Watchful. Awake and ready, lamp lit, for someone coming home. In the Gospels, it means doing today's good, without anxiety about tomorrow.
Your line: ready, not afraid. Like servants awake for someone coming home. Rest well.
